Here, we provide a rigorous evaluation of epoch-wise double descent for a variety of optimizers and
learning rate schedules. We train ResNet18 on CIFAR-10 with data-augmentation and 20% label
noise with three different optimizers—Adam, SGD, SGD + Momentum (momentum set to 0.9) and
three different learning rate schedules—constant, inverse-square root, dynamic drop for differnet
values of initial learning rate. We observe that double-descent occurs reliably for all optimizers and
learning rate schedules and the peak of the double descent curve shifts with the interpolation point.

Figure 4: Model-wise double descent for ResNet18s. Trained on CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10, with
varying label noise. Optimized using Adam with LR 0.0001 for 4K epochs, and data-augmentation.

## Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) — what the corpus says

**Stochastic gradient descent** is the workhorse optimization algorithm for training deep neural networks across this corpus. Several papers touch it from different angles — from its basic definition, to variants, to one paper whose entire contribution is an SGD training schedule, to work analyzing *why* SGD-trained networks behave the way they do.

### What SGD is, and its common variants
SGD "has proved to be an effective way of training deep networks," optimizing the network parameters Θ to minimize the loss; standard variants include **momentum** and **Adagrad** (*Batch Normalization*, `1502.03167`, p. 1). A batch-normalized network can be trained with batch gradient descent, or SGD with a mini-batch of size m > 1, or any of these variants (`1502.03167`, p. 4). A related generalization is **online gradient descent** (Zinkevich, 2003), which moves the current estimate θₜ in the opposite direction of the gradient and arises as a special case of adaptive methods like ADAM (*Practical Bayesian Neural Networks via Adaptive Optimization Methods*, `1811.03679`, pp. 1–2).

### SGDR — a warm-restart schedule *for* SGD (the most SGD-central paper)
The paper most directly about SGD is **SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Restarts** (`1608.03983`). It proposes "a simple warm restart technique for stochastic gradient descent to improve its anytime performance when training deep neural networks," reaching state-of-the-art error of **3.14% on CIFAR-10 and 16.21% on CIFAR-100** (p. 1). Mechanically, a new warm-started run of SGD is simulated once Tᵢ epochs are performed; restarts are **not from scratch** but emulated by increasing the learning rate ηₜ while reusing the old solution xₜ as the initial point, so previously acquired information such as momentum is retained (p. 4). The learning-rate schedule decays ηₜ within each run from a max to 0 (cosine annealing), with restart periods that can double (T_mult = 2) at each restart (p. 2). This schedule later inspired "snapshot ensembles" — taking M model snapshots right before the last M restarts to build an ensemble essentially for free (p. 7).

### SGD as an implicit regularizer (why it generalizes)
*Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization* (`1611.03530`) analyzes SGD's role in generalization. Because "we almost always choose our model as the output of running stochastic gradient descent," and for linear models SGD always converges to a **minimum-norm solution**, the algorithm itself acts as an **implicit regularizer** (p. 3). Concretely, the SGD update wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − ηₜeₜx_{iₜ} keeps the solution in the span of the data points (w = Xᵀα); combined with interpolation this pins down which global minimum SGD selects (p. 9). The same paper notes the striking fact that SGD with unchanged hyperparameters can fit **random labels** perfectly, destroying the image–label relationship yet still driving training loss to zero (p. 4).

### SGD in phenomena studies
- **Deep double descent** (`1912.02292`): epoch-wise double descent occurs reliably across optimizers — Adam, SGD, and SGD+Momentum (0.9) — and across constant / inverse-square-root / dynamic-drop learning-rate schedules; the peak shifts with the interpolation point (p. 18; Fig. 18, p. 19).
- **Grokking** (`2201.02177`): among interventions probed for generalization, the authors contrast **full-batch gradient descent vs. stochastic gradient descent**, along with large/small learning rates (p. 3).
- **Lottery Ticket Hypothesis** (`1803.03635`): the iterative pruning experiments on LeNet/MNIST are run with plain SGD and with **SGD + momentum (0.9)** across various learning rates (Figs. 27–28, pp. 25–26).

### Bottom line
Across this corpus SGD appears as (1) the default training algorithm and its variants (momentum, Adagrad, Adam/online GD) — `1502.03167`, `1811.03679`; (2) the direct subject of an improved training schedule, **SGDR** with cosine-annealed warm restarts — `1608.03983`; and (3) an object of theoretical/empirical study explaining generalization via implicit regularization and phenomena like double descent and grokking — `1611.03530`, `1912.02292`, `2201.02177`, `1803.03635`.

A note on scope: `doc_match_counts` shows ~20 documents contain the phrase, but most others (e.g. `2005.14165`, `1712.00409`, `2203.15556`) mention it only in passing or in reference lists; the documents above carry the substantive SGD content.
